Lecture 22

Step functions, impulses and distributions

Lecture objectives

We define test functions and distributions, differentiate them by moving derivatives onto the test functions, and compute with the step and the delta. We prove the composition rule for δ(g(x)),\dirac(g(x))δ(g(x)), write point sources in curvilinear coordinates and prove that ∇2(1/r)\laplacian(1/r)∇2(1/r) is −4π-4\pi−4π times the three-dimensional delta. Finally we state the standing rules for improper integrals and introduce the rapidly decreasing test functions.

Lecture 8 read its kernel as the motion produced by a force that acts during a very short time. Lectures 2 and 3 met fields whose divergence vanishes wherever the field is defined, that is, off an axis or off a point, while their flux through a surrounding cylinder or sphere does not vanish. Both situations call for an object concentrated at one point: an impulse in time, or a point source in space. No function has these properties. In this lecture we describe such objects, the distributions, by their integrals against smooth test functions. The lecture reads in four stages: impulses, distributions and the struck oscillator (Sections 22.1–22.3); operations and composition (Section 22.4); deltas in space and the source of 1/r1/r1/r (Sections 22.5–22.6); and the standing rules with the tempered class (Sections 22.7–22.8).

22.1 Impulses as limits of short forces

A hammer blow to the oscillator mq¨+bq˙+kq=F(t)m\ddot q+b\dot q+kq=F(t)mq¨​+bq˙​+kq=F(t) of Lecture 9 is a large force that starts at the time τ,\tauτ, lasts the time ε>0\varepsilon>0ε>0 and transfers the momentum p=∫F(t) ⁣dt.p=\int F(t)\dd tp=∫F(t)dt. We model it by a fixed shape, compressed in time and stretched in height so that ppp stays fixed.

22.2 Test functions and distributions

The functions ψ\psiψ that probe a concentrated object are taken as smooth as possible and vanishing outside a bounded set. For an open set Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset\R^dΩ⊂Rd and a continuous function ψ\psiψ on Ω,\OmegaΩ, the support supp⁡ψ\supp\psisuppψ is the closure in Rd\R^dRd of the set of points where ψ≠0,\psi\ne0ψ=0, that is, the set of all limits in Rd\R^dRd of convergent sequences of such points. A set is closed if it contains the limits of all convergent sequences of its points. A function is smooth if all its partial derivatives of all orders exist and are continuous. For a multi-index α=(α1,…,αd)\alpha=(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)α=(α1​,…,αd​) of nonnegative integers we write ∂α=∂1α1⋯∂dαd\partial^\alpha=\partial_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots\partial_d^{\alpha_d}∂α=∂1α1​​⋯∂dαd​​ and ∣α∣=α1+⋯+αd.\abs\alpha=\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_d∣α∣=α1​+⋯+αd​.

Definition 22.3 (Test functions). Let Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset\R^dΩ⊂Rd be open. The space D(Ω)\testspace(\Omega)D(Ω) of test functions consists of the smooth functions ψ:Ω→C\psi:\Omega\to\Cψ:Ω→C whose support is a bounded closed set contained in Ω.\OmegaΩ.

Test functions exist in abundance. GM 11 proved that the function F(t)=e−1/t2,F(t)=\ee^{-1/t^2}F(t)=e−1/t2, with F(0)=0,F(0)=0F(0)=0, is smooth on R\RR and that all its derivatives vanish at 0.00. Hence the function EEE equal to FFF for t>0t>0t>0 and to 000 for t≤0t\le0t≤0 is smooth: by induction, E(n)E^{(n)}E(n) equals F(n)F^{(n)}F(n) for t>0t>0t>0 and 000 for t≤0,t\le0t≤0, and at 000 both one-sided difference quotients of E(n)E^{(n)}E(n) tend to F(n+1)(0)=0.F^{(n+1)}(0)=0F(n+1)(0)=0. The bump ψ1(x)=e2E(1+x)E(1−x)={exp⁡(2−1(1+x)2−1(1−x)2),∣x∣<1,0,∣x∣≥1,\psi_1(x)=\ee^2E(1+x)E(1-x)=\begin{cases}\exp\Bigl(2-\dfrac1{(1+x)^2}-\dfrac1{(1-x)^2}\Bigr),&\abs x<1,\\[1ex]0,&\abs x\ge1,\end{cases}ψ1​(x)=e2E(1+x)E(1−x)=⎩⎨⎧​exp(2−(1+x)21​−(1−x)21​),0,​∣x∣<1,∣x∣≥1,​(22.3) is therefore smooth by the product rule (GM 8). Its support is [−1,1],[-1,1][−1,1], it is positive on (−1,1),(-1,1)(−1,1), and ψ1(0)=1.\psi_1(0)=1ψ1​(0)=1. For a∈Ra\in\Ra∈R and r>0r>0r>0 the function ψ1((x−a)/r)\psi_1((x-a)/r)ψ1​((x−a)/r) is a test function with support [a−r,a+r].[a-r,a+r][a−r,a+r]. In Rd\R^dRd the product ψ1(x1)⋯ψ1(xd)\psi_1(x_1)\cdots\psi_1(x_d)ψ1​(x1​)⋯ψ1​(xd​) is a test function with support [−1,1]d.[-1,1]^d[−1,1]d. A test function equal to 111 on an interval is obtained by integrating two bumps: with c=∫ψ1 ⁣dt,c=\int\psi_1\dd tc=∫ψ1​dt, the smooth function ζ(x)=1c∫−∞x(ψ1(t+2)−ψ1(t−2)) ⁣dt\zeta(x)=\frac1c\int_{-\infty}^x\bigl(\psi_1(t+2)-\psi_1(t-2)\bigr)\dd tζ(x)=c1​∫−∞x​(ψ1​(t+2)−ψ1​(t−2))dt rises from 000 to 111 on [−3,−1],[-3,-1][−3,−1], equals 111 on [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] and returns to 000 on [1,3].[1,3][1,3]. Its translates and dilates, and in Rd\R^dRd the products ζ(x1)⋯ζ(xd),\zeta(x_1)\cdots\zeta(x_d)ζ(x1​)⋯ζ(xd​), equal 111 near any given point.

A concentrated object is a rule that assigns a number to each test function. The rule must be linear, and a small test function with small derivatives must receive a small number.

Definition 22.4 (Distribution). Let Ω⊂Rd\Omega\subset\R^dΩ⊂Rd be open. A distribution on Ω\OmegaΩ is a linear map T:D(Ω)→C,T:\testspace(\Omega)\to\CT:D(Ω)→C, written ψ↦⟨T,ψ⟩,\psi\mapsto\distpair T\psiψ↦⟨T,ψ⟩, with the following property: for every bounded closed set K⊂ΩK\subset\OmegaK⊂Ω there are a constant CK≥0C_K\ge0CK​≥0 and an integer NK≥0N_K\ge0NK​≥0 such that ∣⟨T,ψ⟩∣≤CK∑∣α∣≤NKsup⁡∣∂αψ∣for all ψ∈D(Ω) with supp⁡ψ⊂K.\abs{\distpair T\psi}\le C_K\sum_{\abs\alpha\le N_K}\sup\abs{\partial^\alpha\psi} \qquad\text{for all }\psi\in\testspace(\Omega)\text{ with }\supp\psi\subset K .∣⟨T,ψ⟩∣≤CK​∣α∣≤NK​∑​sup∣∂αψ∣for all ψ∈D(Ω) with suppψ⊂K.(22.4) The distributions on Ω\OmegaΩ form the space D′(Ω).\testspace'(\Omega)D′(Ω).

For d=1d=1d=1 the sum in (22.4) is sup⁡∣ψ∣+sup⁡∣ψ′∣+⋯+sup⁡∣ψ(NK)∣.\sup\abs\psi+\sup\abs{\psi'}+\cdots+\sup\abs{\psi^{(N_K)}}sup∣ψ∣+sup∣ψ′∣+⋯+sup​ψ(NK​)​. The bound (22.4) is the continuity of T,TT, written as an estimate. The pairing ⟨T,ψ⟩\distpair T\psi⟨T,ψ⟩ is linear in ψ,\psiψ, with no complex conjugation, unlike the inner product of Linear Algebra, which is conjugate-linear in its first argument.

The first examples come from functions.

Definition 22.5 (Locally integrable function).

  • A function fff on R\RR is locally integrable if on every bounded interval it is continuous except at finitely many points and its integral over every bounded interval converges absolutely, as an improper integral at the exceptional points (GM 27).

  • A function fff on Rd\R^dRd is locally integrable if it is continuous except at finitely many points pj\vv p_jpj​ (on R3,\R^3R3, alternatively off the zzz-axis), and for every ball BBB the integral of ∣f∣\abs f∣f∣ over BBB with small balls about the pj\vv p_jpj​ (or a thin cylinder r<εr<\varepsilonr<ε about the axis) removed has a finite limit as their radii tend to zero.

Integrals over Rd\R^dRd of such functions are the corresponding limits.

A piecewise continuous function, with finite one-sided limits at its exceptional points, is locally integrable, and so is ∣x∣−1/2.\abs x^{-1/2}∣x∣−1/2. On R3,\R^3R3, spherical coordinates (GM 39) give ∫ε<r<Rr−1 ⁣dV=2π(R2−ε2),\int_{\varepsilon<r<R}r^{-1}\dd V=2\pi(R^2-\varepsilon^2)∫ε<r<R​r−1dV=2π(R2−ε2), so 1/r1/r1/r is locally integrable.

The product fψf\psifψ vanishes outside K,KK, and on BBB with small balls about the pj\vv p_jpj​ removed (for a function continuous off the zzz-axis, a thin cylinder about the axis) we have ∣fψ∣≤sup⁡∣ψ∣ ∣f∣.\abs{f\psi}\le\sup\abs\psi\,\abs f∣fψ∣≤sup∣ψ∣∣f∣. For two choices of radii the integrals of fψf\psifψ differ by at most sup⁡∣ψ∣\sup\abs\psisup∣ψ∣ times the integral of ∣f∣\abs f∣f∣ over the difference of the excised regions, which tends to 000 because the integrals of ∣f∣\abs f∣f∣ converge. So the integral of fψf\psifψ converges (for d=1d=1d=1 this is the comparison test of GM 27), and ∣⟨Tf,ψ⟩∣≤sup⁡∣ψ∣∫B∣f∣ ⁣dV.\abs{\distpair{T_f}\psi}\le\sup\abs\psi\int_B\abs f\dd V∣⟨Tf​,ψ⟩∣≤sup∣ψ∣∫B​∣f∣dV. It is linear in ψ.\psiψ. ■

22.3 Derivatives and the step

For a function f∈C1(R)f\in C^1(\R)f∈C1(R) and a test function ψ,\psiψ, integration by parts (GM 26) on an interval outside of which ψ\psiψ vanishes gives ∫f′ψ ⁣dx=−∫fψ′ ⁣dx,\int f'\psi\dd x=-\int f\psi'\dd x∫f′ψdx=−∫fψ′dx, since the boundary terms are zero. The right side makes sense for every distribution.

Definition 22.10 (Distributional derivative). The derivative of T∈D′(R)T\in\testspace'(\R)T∈D′(R) is given by ⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩.\distpair{T'}\psi=-\distpair T{\psi'}⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩. 22.4 Translation, scaling and composition

Operations on distributions are defined by moving them onto the test function, as for derivatives. For a locally integrable fff on R,\RR, real numbers aaa and c≠0,c\ne0c=0, and a smooth function ggg on R,\RR, the substitutions x↦x+ax\mapsto x+ax↦x+a and x↦x/cx\mapsto x/cx↦x/c give ∫f(x−a)ψ(x) ⁣dx=∫f(x)ψ(x+a) ⁣dx,∫f(cx)ψ(x) ⁣dx=1∣c∣∫f(x)ψ(xc) ⁣dx,\int f(x-a)\psi(x)\dd x=\int f(x)\psi(x+a)\dd x,\qquad \int f(cx)\psi(x)\dd x=\frac1{\abs c}\int f(x)\psi\Bigl(\frac xc\Bigr)\dd x ,∫f(x−a)ψ(x)dx=∫f(x)ψ(x+a)dx,∫f(cx)ψ(x)dx=∣c∣1​∫f(x)ψ(cx​)dx, and ∫(gf)ψ ⁣dx=∫f(gψ) ⁣dx.\int(gf)\psi\dd x=\int f(g\psi)\dd x∫(gf)ψdx=∫f(gψ)dx. 22.5 Deltas in several dimensions and in coordinates

On Rd\R^dRd the derivatives of a distribution are the partial derivatives of Definition 22.10. In particular the Laplacian is given by ⟨∇2T,ψ⟩=⟨T,∇2ψ⟩,\distpair{\laplacian T}\psi=\distpair T{\laplacian\psi}⟨∇2T,ψ⟩=⟨T,∇2ψ⟩, since each ∂j2\partial_j^2∂j2​ moves with two sign changes. 22.7 Standing rules for improper integrals

Lectures 23–28 exchange limits, derivatives and improper integrals (GM 27) over intervals J,JJ, J1J_1J1​ and J2,J_2J2​, possibly unbounded. A function on JJJ is piecewise continuous if on every bounded subinterval it is continuous except at finitely many points, with finite one-sided limits there.

Theorem 22.19 (Standing rules for improper integrals · cited). The following rules hold for piecewise continuous functions on the intervals J,JJ, J1J_1J1​ and J2.J_2J2​. In each rule an exceptional set is a set with finitely many points in each bounded subinterval.

  • Dominated limits. (a) Sequences. Then Φ(λ)=∫JF(λ,x) ⁣dx\Phi(\lambda)=\int_JF(\lambda,x)\dd xΦ(λ)=∫J​F(λ,x)dx converges absolutely for every λ∈Λ,\lambda\in\Lambdaλ∈Λ, Φ\PhiΦ is C1C^1C1 and Φ′(λ)=∫J∂λF(λ,x) ⁣dx.\Phi'(\lambda)=\int_J\partial_\lambda F(\lambda,x)\dd x .Φ′(λ)=∫J​∂λ​F(λ,x)dx.

Suppose that (i) fff is continuous on J1×J2J_1\times J_2J1​×J2​ except on finitely many straight lines in each bounded rectangle, such as lines x=const,x=\text{const}x=const, y=consty=\text{const}y=const or x−y=const;x-y=\text{const}x−y=const; (ii) for every xxx outside an exceptional set the inner integral ∫J2∣f(x,y)∣ ⁣dy\int_{J_2}\abs{f(x,y)}\dd y∫J2​​∣f(x,y)∣dy converges, and for every yyy outside an exceptional set the inner integral ∫J1∣f(x,y)∣ ⁣dx\int_{J_1}\abs{f(x,y)}\dd x∫J1​​∣f(x,y)∣dx converges; (iii) these inner integrals, and those of fff itself, are piecewise continuous functions of xxx and of y,yy, respectively. If f≥0,f\ge0f≥0, the two iterated integrals are equal; they may both be +∞.+\infty+∞. If ∫J1(∫J2∣f∣ ⁣dy) ⁣dx<∞,\int_{J_1}\bigl(\int_{J_2}\abs f\dd y\bigr)\dd x<\infty∫J1​​(∫J2​​∣f∣dy)dx<∞, then ∫J1(∫J2f(x,y) ⁣dy) ⁣dx=∫J2(∫J1f(x,y) ⁣dx) ⁣dy,\int_{J_1}\Bigl(\int_{J_2}f(x,y)\dd y\Bigr)\dd x=\int_{J_2}\Bigl(\int_{J_1}f(x,y)\dd x\Bigr)\dd y ,∫J1​​(∫J2​​f(x,y)dy)dx=∫J2​​(∫J1​​f(x,y)dx)dy, both sides converging absolutely.

Hypothesis (iii) of I3 makes the outer integrals improper integrals in the sense of GM 27, so that both iterated integrals are defined. Lines x−y=constx-y=\text{const}x−y=const occur in the convolution integrals of Lectures 25 and 26. The sibling course Real and Complex Analysis proves rules I1 and I2 for the Lebesgue integral and cites rule I3: rule I1 is AN 3’s theorem “Dominated convergence” with the sequential criterion of GM 5 (of GM 36 for a complex parameter), rule I2 is the differentiation part of AN 4’s theorem “Parameter integrals”, and rule I3 is AN 4’s theorem “M4: Fubini–Tonelli”, which AN cites. By AN 3’s cited theorem “M3: agreement with calculus” the Lebesgue integral of a function integrable on compact subintervals equals its absolutely convergent improper integral, so the rules hold for our integrals. A conditionally convergent integral such as Si⁡(∞)=π/2\Si(\infty)=\pi/2Si(∞)=π/2 of Lecture 20 is outside these rules and is treated by hand where it occurs.

We use the rules as GM 38 uses its standing fact M: they are cited, not proved in this course, and every use names the rule. If the hypotheses of I1(b) hold, with Λ0=Λ,\Lambda_0=\LambdaΛ0​=Λ, at every point λ0\lambda_0λ0​ of an interval Λ\LambdaΛ or of an open set Λ⊂C,\Lambda\subset\CΛ⊂C, with a dominating ggg for each λ0,\lambda_0λ0​, then λ↦∫JF(λ,x) ⁣dx\lambda\mapsto\int_JF(\lambda,x)\dd xλ↦∫J​F(λ,x)dx is continuous on Λ,\LambdaΛ, by AN 3’s dominated convergence and the sequential criterion (GM 5; GM 36 for a complex parameter).

22.8 Rapidly decreasing tests and tempered distributions

Fourier transforms turn a function with bounded support into one without it, so Lectures 23 and 24 need tests that decay with all their derivatives.

Definition 22.20 (Rapidly decreasing functions). The space S(R)\Schwartz(\R)S(R) consists of the smooth functions ψ:R→C\psi:\R\to\Cψ:R→C for which every function xmψ(n)(x),x^m\psi^{(n)}(x)xmψ(n)(x), with integers m,n≥0,m,n\ge0m,n≥0, is bounded on R.\RR. We write ∥ψ∥m,n=sup⁡x∈R∣xmψ(n)(x)∣.\norm{\psi}_{m,n}=\sup_{x\in\R}\abs{x^m\psi^{(n)}(x)} .∥ψ∥m,n​=x∈Rsup​​xmψ(n)(x)​. These numbers are the seminorms of ψ.\psiψ. On Rd\R^dRd the space S(Rd)\Schwartz(\R^d)S(Rd) is defined in the same way, with monomials x1β1⋯xdβdx_1^{\beta_1}\cdots x_d^{\beta_d}x1β1​​⋯xdβd​​ and derivatives ∂α.\partial^\alpha∂α.

Every test function is rapidly decreasing, so D(R)⊂S(R).\testspace(\R)\subset\Schwartz(\R)D(R)⊂S(R). The Gaussian e−x2\ee^{-x^2}e−x2 is rapidly decreasing but not a test function: by induction, its nnnth derivative is a polynomial times e−x2,\ee^{-x^2}e−x2, and xje−x2→0x^j\ee^{-x^2}\to0xje−x2→0 as ∣x∣→∞\abs x\to\infty∣x∣→∞ by the bound ew≥wN/N!\ee^w\ge w^N/N!ew≥wN/N! of GM 11 with w=x2w=x^2w=x2 and 2N>j.2N>j2N>j.

Definition 22.21 (Tempered distribution). A tempered distribution is a linear map T:S(R)→CT:\Schwartz(\R)\to\CT:S(R)→C for which there are a constant C≥0C\ge0C≥0 and an integer N≥0N\ge0N≥0 with ∣⟨T,ψ⟩∣≤C∑m,n=0N∥ψ∥m,nfor all ψ∈S(R).\abs{\distpair T\psi}\le C\sum_{m,n=0}^N\norm{\psi}_{m,n}\qquad\text{for all }\psi\in\Schwartz(\R).∣⟨T,ψ⟩∣≤Cm,n=0∑N​∥ψ∥m,n​for all ψ∈S(R).(22.20) The tempered distributions form the space S′(R);\tempered(\R)S′(R); on Rd\R^dRd the definition is the same.

A tempered distribution restricts to a distribution: if ψ∈D(R)\psi\in\testspace(\R)ψ∈D(R) vanishes outside [−L,L],[-L,L][−L,L], then ∥ψ∥m,n≤Lmsup⁡∣ψ(n)∣,\norm{\psi}_{m,n}\le L^m\sup\abs{\psi^{(n)}}∥ψ∥m,n​≤Lmsup​ψ(n)​, which gives (22.4).

Proposition 22.22 (Examples of tempered distributions). The following define tempered distributions on R.\RR.

  • A locally integrable fff with ∣f(x)∣≤C0(1+∣x∣)ℓ\abs{f(x)}\le C_0(1+\abs x)^\ell∣f(x)∣≤C0​(1+∣x∣)ℓ for ∣x∣≥1,\abs x\ge1∣x∣≥1, for constants C0C_0C0​ and an integer ℓ≥0;\ell\ge0ℓ≥0; in particular every polynomial, Θ\HeavisideΘ and sgn⁡.\sgnsgn.

  • The deltas δ(x−a)\dirac(x-a)δ(x−a) and every derivative of a tempered distribution, defined by ⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩.\distpair{T'}\psi=-\distpair T{\psi'}⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩.

Proof. For the first item, split the integral at ∣x∣=1:\abs x=1∣x∣=1: ∫∣fψ∣ ⁣dx≤sup⁡∣ψ∣∫−11∣f∣ ⁣dx+C0sup⁡x((1+∣x∣)ℓ+2∣ψ(x)∣)∫∣x∣≥1 ⁣dx(1+∣x∣)2.\int\abs{f\psi}\dd x\le\sup\abs\psi\int_{-1}^1\abs f\dd x+C_0\sup_x\bigl((1+\abs x)^{\ell+2}\abs{\psi(x)}\bigr)\int_{\abs x\ge1}\frac{\dd x}{(1+\abs x)^2}.∫∣fψ∣dx≤sup∣ψ∣∫−11​∣f∣dx+C0​xsup​((1+∣x∣)ℓ+2∣ψ(x)∣)∫∣x∣≥1​(1+∣x∣)2dx​. The last integral is 1,11, and by the binomial formula the supremum is at most ∑m=0ℓ+2(ℓ+2m)∥ψ∥m,0.\sum_{m=0}^{\ell+2}\binom{\ell+2}m\norm{\psi}_{m,0}∑m=0ℓ+2​(mℓ+2​)∥ψ∥m,0​. For the second item, ∣ψ(a)∣≤∥ψ∥0,0\abs{\psi(a)}\le\norm{\psi}_{0,0}∣ψ(a)∣≤∥ψ∥0,0​ and ∥ψ′∥m,n=∥ψ∥m,n+1.\norm{\psi'}_{m,n}=\norm{\psi}_{m,n+1}∥ψ′∥m,n​=∥ψ∥m,n+1​. ■

Not every distribution is tempered.

Proposition 22.23 (The exponential is not tempered). There is no tempered distribution TTT with ⟨T,ψ⟩=∫exψ(x) ⁣dx\distpair T\psi=\int\ee^x\psi(x)\dd x⟨T,ψ⟩=∫exψ(x)dx for every ψ∈D(R).\psi\in\testspace(\R)ψ∈D(R).

Proof. Suppose that such a TTT exists, with CCC and NNN as in (22.20). Let ψn(x)=ψ1(x−n)\psi_n(x)=\psi_1(x-n)ψn​(x)=ψ1​(x−n) for n=1,2,…,n=1,2,\ldotsn=1,2,…, with the bump (22.3). Then ⟨T,ψn⟩=∫n−1n+1exψ1(x−n) ⁣dx=c en,c=∫−11euψ1(u) ⁣du>0.\distpair T{\psi_n}=\int_{n-1}^{n+1}\ee^x\psi_1(x-n)\dd x=c\,\ee^n,\qquad c=\int_{-1}^1\ee^u\psi_1(u)\dd u>0 .⟨T,ψn​⟩=∫n−1n+1​exψ1​(x−n)dx=cen,c=∫−11​euψ1​(u)du>0. On the support of ψn\psi_nψn​ we have ∣x∣≤n+1,\abs x\le n+1∣x∣≤n+1, so ∥ψn∥m,j≤(n+1)msup⁡∣ψ1(j)∣.\norm{\psi_n}_{m,j}\le(n+1)^m\sup\abs{\psi_1^{(j)}}∥ψn​∥m,j​≤(n+1)msup​ψ1(j)​​. Hence c en≤C′(n+1)Nc\,\ee^n\le C'(n+1)^Ncen≤C′(n+1)N for every n,nn, with a constant C′.C'C′. This contradicts the bound en≥nN+1/(N+1)!\ee^n\ge n^{N+1}/(N+1)!en≥nN+1/(N+1)! of GM 11, by which en/(n+1)N→∞.\ee^n/(n+1)^N\to\inftyen/(n+1)N→∞. ■

So ex\ee^xex has no Fourier transform in the sense of Lecture 24.

Summary

A distribution is a linear rule that assigns numbers to smooth test functions of bounded support, with the bound (22.4). Locally integrable functions define distributions, and so does δ(x−a),\dirac(x-a)δ(x−a), which is not a function. Derivatives act on the test functions, so a jump produces a delta in the derivative.

  • Classes: D(Ω),\testspace(\Omega)D(Ω), smooth with bounded support in Ω;\OmegaΩ; S(R),\Schwartz(\R)S(R), smooth with every xmψ(n)x^m\psi^{(n)}xmψ(n) bounded; distributions satisfy (22.4), tempered ones (22.20); ex\ee^xex is not tempered.

  • Calculus: ⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩;\distpair{T'}\psi=-\distpair T{\psi'}⟨T′,ψ⟩=−⟨T,ψ′⟩; Θ′=δ;\Heaviside'=\diracΘ′=δ; (Tf)′=Tf′+∑j[f]xjδ(x−xj);(T_f)'=T_{f'}+\sum_j[f]_{x_j}\dirac(x-x_j)(Tf​)′=Tf′​+∑j​[f]xj​​δ(x−xj​); gδa=g(a)δa;g\dirac_a=g(a)\dirac_agδa​=g(a)δa​; δ(cx)=δ(x)/∣c∣;\dirac(cx)=\dirac(x)/\abs cδ(cx)=δ(x)/∣c∣; δ(g(x))=∑jδ(x−xj)/∣g′(xj)∣\dirac(g(x))=\sum_j\dirac(x-x_j)/\abs{g'(x_j)}δ(g(x))=∑j​δ(x−xj​)/∣g′(xj​)∣ for simple zeros.

  • Sources: δ(3)(x−x0)=δ(r−r0)δ(θ−θ0)δ(φ−φ0)/(r02sin⁡θ0)\dirac^{(3)}(\vv x-\vv x_0)=\dirac(r-r_0)\dirac(\theta-\theta_0)\dirac(\varphi-\varphi_0)/(r_0^2\sin\theta_0)δ(3)(x−x0​)=δ(r−r0​)δ(θ−θ0​)δ(φ−φ0​)/(r02​sinθ0​) off the zzz-axis; ∇2(1/r)=−4πδ(3).\laplacian(1/r)=-4\pi\dirac^{(3)}∇2(1/r)=−4πδ(3).

  • Rules: dominated limits (I1), differentiation under the integral sign (I2) and Fubini–Tonelli (I3), for absolutely convergent improper integrals.

Lecture 23 defines the Fourier transform and proves its inversion formula.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Let ψ\psiψ be a smooth compactly supported test function equal to x+3x+3x+3 near both x=−2x=-2x=−2 and x=2x=2x=2. Find ⟨δ(x2−4),ψ⟩\distpair{\dirac(x^2-4)}{\psi}⟨δ(x2−4),ψ⟩. Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Find the simple zeros and the absolute derivative at each zero.

For g(x)=x2−4g(x)=x^2-4g(x)=x2−4 the zeros are −2-2−2 and 222, and ∣g′∣=4\abs{g'}=4∣g′∣=4 at both. The delta of ggg therefore samples the test function at both zeros with weight 1/41/41/4. The result is (1+5)/4=3/2(1+5)/4=3/2(1+5)/4=3/2. Using the signed derivative would give one negative weight even though both local changes of variables use an absolute Jacobian.

2. For f(t)=(2+t)Θ(t)f(t)=(2+t)\Heaviside(t)f(t)=(2+t)Θ(t), what is the derivative in the sense of distributions?

Hint. Find the ordinary derivative on each open side and the change from the left one-sided limit to the right one-sided limit.

The ordinary derivative is zero for t<0t<0t<0 and one for t>0t>0t>0, giving Θ(t)\Heaviside(t)Θ(t). Integration by parts on the two sides gives a delta with coefficient equal to the right limit minus the left limit, here 2−0=22-0=22−0=2. A negative coefficient reverses the jump. Keeping only the step drops the jump, and keeping only the delta drops the ordinary derivative.

3. On a cylindrical coordinate patch containing x0\vv x_0x0​ with coordinates (2,φ0,z0)(2,\varphi_0,z_0)(2,φ0​,z0​), write a unit point source as Aδ(r−2)δ(φ−φ0)δ(z−z0)A\dirac(r-2)\dirac(\varphi-\varphi_0)\dirac(z-z_0)Aδ(r−2)δ(φ−φ0​)δ(z−z0​) against the physical volume r ⁣dr ⁣dφ ⁣dzr\dd r\dd\varphi\dd zrdrdφdz. What is AAA?

Hint. Apply the source to a test function and keep the radial factor in the volume element.

The deltas evaluate the product of the test function and rrr at the source. The result is 2Aψ(x0)2A\psi(\vv x_0)2Aψ(x0​), which must equal ψ(x0)\psi(\vv x_0)ψ(x0​). Thus A=1/2A=1/2A=1/2. A coefficient of 111 omits the Jacobian, 222 multiplies by it instead of dividing, and 1/41/41/4 uses a squared radial factor as in spherical coordinates.

4. Why does the locally integrable function ex\ee^xex fail to define a tempered distribution on R\RR?

Hint. Translate a nonzero compactly supported test function and compare the pairing with the bounds required by Schwartz continuity.

Shifting a fixed nonzero nonnegative compactly supported test function by a>0a>0a>0 multiplies its pairing by ea\ee^aea. Every fixed Schwartz seminorm of the shifted function grows at most like a power of 1+a1+a1+a. No finite seminorm bound can dominate that exponential. Local integrability gives a distribution on compactly supported tests. The constant function one is outside the Schwartz class, so its integral cannot test temperedness. Unboundedness alone allows tempered examples such as polynomials.
